title: Six typefaces and their stories: Garamond, Futura, Times New Roman, Courier, Helvetica, Comic Sans

facts.text: Claude Garamond cut punches for metal type in Paris in the 1500s; most of his designs date from the 1530s to the 1560s.
After Garamond died in 1561, his punches were sold and spread across Europe.
Garamond-style typefaces are valued for comfortable long reading, and modern versions are used in many books, such as U.S. editions of Harry Potter.
German designer Paul Renner began work on Futura in 1924, and it was released in 1927.
Futura's letters are built from geometric shapes: circles, triangles, and squares.
In 1969, Futura was used on the plaque that the Apollo 11 astronauts left on the Moon.
The Times of London asked Stanley Morison for a better typeface; Times New Roman first appeared in the newspaper on October 3, 1932.
Times New Roman was designed to stay easy to read while fitting more words on each line.
Times New Roman became a common choice for school assignments and papers.
Howard Kettler designed Courier for IBM in 1955 to look like the output of a typewriter.
Courier is monospaced: every character takes up the same width.
IBM did not keep exclusive rights to Courier, so it spread across the typewriter industry and became the most common typewriter typeface for decades.
Helvetica was created in Switzerland by Max Miedinger and Eduard Hoffmann and launched in 1957; they wanted a neutral design.
The name Helvetica, adopted in 1960, means Swiss in Latin.
Helvetica has been used on New York subway signs since 1989, in many company logos, and on the side of NASA's Space Shuttle.
Many designers find Helvetica boring or unoriginal, even though it is still among the most popular typefaces.
In 1994, Vincent Connare at Microsoft designed Comic Sans for cartoon characters that spoke in speech bubbles, because the default font looked too formal.
Comic Sans was inspired by the lettering in comic books.
Comic Sans has been widely mocked, yet scientists at CERN, a physics laboratory in Europe, used it to announce evidence of the Higgs boson.
